**A voice assistant is a streaming conversation, not a text chatbot with audio attached.** The system listens while the user speaks, forms partial interpretations, decides when the turn is complete, generates a response, and starts speaking before every downstream component has necessarily finished.

**Walk through “Set a timer for… actually, ten minutes.”** Early speech recognition may produce an incomplete or revised transcript. A speculative intent detector can prepare a timer action, but should not execute the wrong duration before the correction is resolved. Voice activity detection detects speech/silence; it does not by itself understand that the user has finished their thought.

**Why endpointing matters.** Waiting too long after the user stops makes the assistant feel sluggish. Ending too early interrupts the user or acts on an incomplete request. Measure this tradeoff on real conversational pauses, accents, noise, and interruptions rather than only clean prerecorded sentences.

Streaming ASR, model output, and text-to-speech can overlap to reduce perceived delay. [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.04356) However, if the user interrupts, queued audio must stop and conversation state must reflect what was actually heard, not the entire response that had been generated internally. Pending actions need cancellation or explicit completion state as well.

**Use a timeline for evaluation.** Measure capture delay, transcription revisions, end-of-turn delay, first response audio, and interruption recovery. A fast language model can still produce a slow assistant if endpointing or synthesis dominates. Test tool actions separately from conversational responses because an awkward spoken phrase is reversible, while an incorrectly executed action may not be.

**Technical details and references.**

Pipeline audio capture into echo cancellation, voice activity detection, streaming ASR, dialogue inference, and chunked TTS. VAD detects acoustic speech activity; semantic turn detection additionally estimates whether the utterance is complete. Partial ASR hypotheses can start speculative intent/retrieval, but irreversible actions should wait for confirmed intent.

Every turn and audio chunk carries a monotonic sequence/turn ID. On barge-in, cancel active generation, stop queued playback, and discard late chunks from the old turn. Update conversation history to reflect audio actually played, not the entire generated answer. Maintain backpressure so a slow network or speaker does not accumulate seconds of stale audio.

Budget end-of-speech-to-first-audio latency across endpointing, reasoning, and synthesis; this is distinct from ASR word latency. Evaluate interruption recovery, false turn endings, word error rate by accent/noise, and task completion. A direct speech model can avoid some text-stage latency but changes observability and control; a modular ASR/LLM/TTS stack is easier to diagnose and replace. Consent, retention, and redaction rules apply to recorded audio as well as transcripts.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** Turn latency is the interval from the user's meaningful completion to the assistant's first useful audio, not merely model inference time. Measure endpointing delay, partial-transcript revision, response generation, synthesis, and playback jointly. Barge-in requires canceling queued audio and pending actions, with conversation state reflecting what was actually played to the user. [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.04356)

For the implementation or system context discussed above, see [1](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/realtime) and [2](https://docs.pipecat.ai/guides/introduction).
